sections.heading: Problem-level score.
sections.text: For problem p, let S_{p} be the set of successful solutions and T_{p} the set of private tests. Let \binom{S_{p}}{2} denote all unordered pairs of distinct solutions. For each test t\in T_{p}, we compute \mathrm{DMPD} for every pair (i,j)\in\binom{S_{p}}{2} using the corresponding unit-peak MPPs. The problem-level instability is the mean over pairs and tests: (4) D_{p}\;=\;\frac{1}{\left|\binom{S_{p}}{2}\right|\cdot|T_{p}|}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in\binom{S_{p}}{2}}\;\sum_{t\in T_{p}}\;\mathrm{DMPD}\!\left(P_{p,i,t},\,P_{p,j,t}\right).

sections.heading: Model Instability Score (MIS)
sections.text: Over a set of problems \mathcal{P}, we report the macro MIS as the unweighted average of problem scores: (5) \mathrm{MIS}_{\text{macro}}\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}D_{p}. When problems vary widely in the number of successful solutions or tests, we additionally report a micro average that weights by the number of evaluated pairs and tests: (6) \mathrm{MIS}_{\text{micro}}\;=\;\frac{\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\left|\binom{S_{p}}{2}\right||T_{p}|\,D_{p}}{\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\left|\binom{S_{p}}{2}\right||T_{p}|}.

sections.heading: Language and runtime specificity.
sections.text: All experiments use Python and instrument application-level allocations via tracemalloc under CPython’s reference counting plus cyclic GC ( Stinner, 2014 ; Python Software Foundation, 2025 ) . These choices suppress RSS/allocator noise but also bias us toward Python’s memory semantics. Other ecosystems differ materially e.g., JVM and .NET employ moving, generational collectors with tunable heuristics ( Jayasena et al., 2015 ; Jones et al., 2023 ) , Go prioritizes low-latency concurrent GC ( Hudson, 2015 ) , while Rust enforces ownership and largely avoids GC ( Klabnik and Nichols, 2023 ) . Such differences can change allocation shapes and, therefore, DTW distances. Low-level allocator behavior and fragmentation also vary by platform ( Nethercote and Seward, 2007 ; Jones et al., 2023 ) . Hence, our scores cannot be transferred to other languages without replication.

sections.heading: Benchmark vs. real systems.
sections.text: We evaluate on simple competitive coding style problems (CodeContests, BigOBench), not on production services. Real software is more complex and introduces frameworks, concurrency, and deployment constraints (containers, limits, autoscaling) that may interact with memory trajectories and tail behavior ( Dean and Barroso, 2013 ) . External validity is a general challenge in SE empiricism ( Wohlin and Runeson, 2012 ; Kitchenham et al., 2007 ) . Our findings motivate, but do not replace, validation on industrial repositories and end-to-end workloads.

sections.heading: Sampling budget and statistical power.
sections.text: We cap generations to each problem at N{=}5 correct generations and at most r{=}10 private tests. This modest budget limits \binom{k}{2} pairwise comparisons, can miss long-tail behaviors, and increases the variance of D_{p} and \mathrm{MIS}. Although we fix seeds and use a single-bin policy to improve repeatability (for Mercury scaling test), estimates remain sensitive to which samples happen to be drawn. We report medians/IQRs and perform sensitivity checks, but larger N/r or explicit uncertainty estimates would yield tighter measurements.
